SALINA, Kan. – In 1976, Wes and Dana Jackson launched The Land Institute as a nonprofit school to teach a small group of students ways to grow food that respected nature, conserved energy and water, and managed wastes. As one of the nation’s first regional nonprofit environmental and farm research organizations devoted to land stewardship, the Institute set sail in the powerful current of alternative ideas and new organizations in that era that were determined to change how America operated. You recall that only six years prior 20 million Americans held public demonstrations in support of the first Earth Day. In 1978, though, just two years after it opened, Wes Jackson, a plant geneticist, dramatically shifted the Institute’s work to basic science and plant research devoted to accomplishing an immense feat. He sought to completely overturn the 10,000-year-old system of grain production. Instead of plowing and seeding and harvesting annually, practices that depleted the soil, and wasted water and energy, Jackson proposed developing crops that were planted once, developed deep roots, grew back year after year like perennial flowers or apple trees, and were much less vulnerable to insects, diseases, and droughts. Sign up His idea was inspired by the tallgrass prairie of his native Kansas – a landscape decorated with big bluestem, Indiangrass, switchgrass, and little bluestem. Jackson began hiring top plant scientists to develop the new crops and gave the Institute 50 to 100 years to prove that a “perennial” grain production system was achievable. That improbable merger of instinct, vision, and science gradually evolved and eventually yielded a breakthrough of stunning global achievement that 1,000 people celebrated here in late September at the Prairie Festival, marking The Land Institute’s 50 th year.
